Consult Summary:
- Acute 3-day history of watery then very loose diarrhoea with profuse vomiting and subjective fever, periumbilical abdominal pain, household contact with similar illness; clinician suspects infectious gastroenteritis and recommended stool testing and assessment for dehydration.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Acute diarrhoea and vomiting for 3 days.
  - Subjective high temperature ("literally boiling").
  - Periumbilical abdominal pain described as very tender to touch; intermittent and associated with urgency to defecate.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began 3 days ago.
  - Vomiting this morning approximately 2 hours before the call.
  - Passed urine ~1 hour before the call.
  - ORS (oral rehydration salts) taken ~3 times daily for past 2 days but largely vomited.
  - Diarrhoea frequency: lost overall count; at least 4 times today.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Eating/drinking provokes vomiting; advised to take very small sips of ORS.
  - No effective relief reported; symptoms not improving.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Nausea, repeated vomiting, subjective fever.
  - No rash reported.
  - No blood in stool or urine reported.
  - Urination occurring (patient reports passing urine).
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No reported prior similar episodes of diarrhoea or chronic GI disease.
  - No reported recent travel.
  - No reported bloody stool, rash, or other systemic complaints.
  - Not sexually active; not on contraception.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported.
- Occasional menstrual cramps; last period ~2 weeks ago.
- No prior abdominal surgeries or chronic GI diagnoses reported.

Medications:
- Vitamin D — taken daily; dose/route not documented.
- Ibuprofen — used occasionally for menstrual cramps; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- No other regular medications reported.

Allergies:
- Not recorded / not mentioned in the consultation.

Social History:
- Lives with brother and mother.
- Brother has had similar symptoms for several days; patient reports a wider school outbreak per brother.
- Occupation: graphics designer; working from home today due to illness.
- Smoking: does not smoke.
- Alcohol: occasional (reports having "a pint from time to time").
- No recreational drug use reported.

Family History:
- Household contact (brother) with similar diarrhoeal illness; no other family history documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Patient-reported marked tenderness over the periumbilical (navel) area; no objective physical exam documented by clinician.

Investigations:
- None performed during the call.
- Clinician recommended:
  - Stool sample for microbiology to exclude bacterial pathogens (to be obtained at clinic visit if possible; otherwise posted to patient).
  - Clinical assessment for dehydration (to be done in clinic).
- No lab values or imaging available.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Most likely acute infectious gastroenteritis (viral most likely) with ongoing vomiting and risk of dehydration; bacterial or toxin-mediated foodborne illness also possible — stool testing and hydration assessment recommended.

DDx Integration (brief):
- Viral gastroenteritis — High likelihood.
  - Supporting: Acute watery diarrhoea then loose stools, prominent vomiting, subjective fever, household contact/outbreak.
  - Opposing/concern: Persistent inability to retain fluids raising dehydration risk and focal periumbilical tenderness (but not inconsistent).
- Bacterial gastroenteritis — Medium likelihood.
  - Supporting: Fever, ongoing symptoms >48–72 hours and not improving with ORS; clinician advised stool testing to rule out treatable bacteria.
  - Opposing: No bloody stool reported; household spread and vomiting favor viral/toxin causes.
- Foodborne toxin (preformed toxin) — Medium likelihood.
  - Supporting: Prominent vomiting and possible clustered cases.
  - Opposing: No clear shared meal history; illness has persisted several days.

Issue 1: Acute gastroenteritis (most likely viral)
- Assessment:
  - Acute onset watery then very loose diarrhoea, vomiting, subjective fever, periumbilical crampy pain; household contact with similar illness consistent with viral gastroenteritis.
- Plan:
  - Arrange urgent clinic appointment for assessment (support line to book — clinician indicated they would arrange).
  - Obtain stool sample at clinic for microbiological testing to exclude bacterial causes.
  - Provide advice for symptomatic care: small, frequent sips of ORS to try to maintain hydration; simple bland foods if tolerated (toast/biscuits).
  - Avoid foods likely to worsen diarrhoea (patient advised to avoid fruit, vegetables, milk).
  - Safety net: If symptoms worsen or patient becomes more unwell, go to Emergency Department (A&E) urgently.

Issue 2: Inability to tolerate oral fluids / risk of dehydration
- Assessment:
  - Repeated vomiting and inability to retain liquids despite ORS; passed urine ~1 hour prior suggesting not yet severely dehydrated but at risk.
- Plan:
  - Clinical assessment of hydration status in clinic (vitals, examination, consideration of need for IV fluids if dehydrated).
  - Continue attempting small-volume ORS sips frequently; avoid large boluses that provoke vomiting.
  - If vomiting persists and oral rehydration fails, escalate to A&E for possible IV rehydration.

Issue 3: Need to identify possible bacterial or toxin causes
- Assessment:
  - Stool testing recommended because symptoms have persisted several days without improvement and to rule out treatable bacterial pathogens; foodborne toxin possible if common exposure.
- Plan:
  - Collect stool sample at clinic for culture/analysis and send to lab.
  - If bacterial pathogen identified, follow-up to arrange appropriate antimicrobial treatment as indicated.
  - If cluster or outbreak suspected, consider public health notification per local protocol (not documented as completed in consult).

General plan items:
- Appointment to be arranged through support line; patient to attend clinic urgently for stool sample and hydration check.
- Continue conservative measures at home (small sips of ORS, simple bland diet) until seen.
- Clear safety-netting: attend A&E if condition deteriorates (worsening vomiting, signs of severe dehydration, high persistent fever, confusion, reduced urine output).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected items: objective vital signs (temperature, pulse, BP), formal abdominal exam findings, stool test results, documented allergies, full medication doses/routes.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted — DDx supports the clinician's impression of likely viral gastroenteritis with bacterial/toxin causes as alternatives.
- Transcript quality: Generally audible and intelligible; short gaps/overlaps when confirming identity and some brief pauses during history-taking.
